assessment: One linked mechanism hypothesis merits a bounded sample test. Combined timing, reported missing parts and insertion retries do not establish their causes or prove that removing workshop assembly will help.

openings.claim: Hypothesis: full workshop assembly creates demand for insertion retries and arrangement checking. In a counterfactual forbidding workshop preassembly, supply an order-specific partition kit on a compartment-count checklist whose part silhouettes and orientation marks also form the customer assembly map. Preserve the existing base, partition geometry, selected count and exterior color. Hybrid parents are physical completeness checking and layout-specific instruction; their interaction makes the checked inventory itself the assembly interface.
openings.delta: Change the workshop/customer relationship from delivering a completed arrangement to delivering a verified arrangement kit. Remove the dependency on workshop insertion as the verification interface. Its former obligations are complete and correct inventory, fit verification, correct arrangement, retention during transport and protection. Replace them with order-to-parts matching, silhouette/count checking, sampled insertion-fit checks, a map for the exact ordered layout, and secured protective packing. Replacement dependencies also include legible orientation cues, accurate map preparation, customer insertion ability, available packing materials and an affordable preparation process. Sample checks may fail to replace unit-level fit verification.
openings.prediction: If preassembly generates avoidable work, removing it reduces total workshop time even after kit checking and packing are counted; customer short-partition placement errors need not increase with an exact-layout map. Increased customer failures or replacement checking time would contradict the proposed benefit.
openings.probe: Use the 15 sample allowance across all three compartment counts to compare matched assembled and kit workflows, timing selection, insertion, verification, map preparation and packing separately. Have ten participants try an assigned workflow unaided; record completeness, arrangement errors and insertion difficulty. Inspect transport retention, footprint and assortment capacity. Cost preparation and recurring materials and check delivery feasibility before any pilot change. Samples screen feasibility; the 60-unit pilot must independently meet the stated success measures.
assumptions: Maps and packing can be prepared within 500 initial and 0.40 recurring units and the fixed delivery date.
Existing reversible slots remain usable by customers.
Kit protection and alternative checks can fulfill the former assembly obligations without increasing missing or incorrect parts.
